title: iTMS Intro 2003 2003-04-28
speaker: Steve Jobs
content:
Good morning.

Thank you. Thank you very much for coming this morning. We have some really exciting things to announce. So let's just get right into it. As you know, Apple's strategy is to innovate. And uh I just like to review a few things that we've launched recently. The uh 12-inch PowerBook, the world's smallest full-featured notebook computer, introduced in January. Alongside it, the world's first 17-inch notebook computer, the 17-inch PowerBook. Uh we've started shipping these in volume and customers are loving them. Reviewers are loving them. I just want to show you one review uh by by a hard critic, Walt Mossberg at the Wall Street Journal.

So, it's it's nice that other people are noticing. Now, on the software side, we launched Safari, our own browser in January as a beta. We're on our second beta and we've had over 3 million downloads of Safari. We could not be happier. This is going very, very well. And we launched iLife, a new incarnation of our digital hub applications, new versions of iPhoto, iMovie and iDVD, and this has gone extremely well too. And Keynote, our presentation program.

Thank you very much. My presentation is in it today. And recently, we've just launched Final Cut 4, the fourth generation of what has become now the most popular pro video editing app in the world. So, this is all of this in only the first four months. Today, we're going to innovate some more and this time in music. Now, when Apple got into digital music, it was almost two and a half years ago. And to announce our entry, we were not the first into it, but when we decided to get into it, we came on strong and we ran an ad called Rip Mix Burn. And let me go ahead and run it for you now.

So, that ad got a certain amount of attention. And uh it wasn't just an ad though, because we introduced iTunes, uh our digital music jukebox and this quickly became one of the most popular digital music jukeboxes in the world. And it led us to a remarkable device called the iPod. And uh this has revolutionized portable music listening. Now, because of these things and some other things that we've contributed to the recording industry, uh Apple was honored with the first Grammy ever awarded to a computer company last year. So, this is where we've been and until today are. Let me go back though to Rip Mix Burn. There was some confusion about this primarily from people that didn't have teenage kids living at home about what rip really meant. Some people thought it meant rip off. Didn't mean that at all. So let's go take a look at what Rip Mix Burn really means. Okay? Rip actually means to take a physical CD and rip the bits off of it and put them on your hard disk. That's what it means to everyone under 30. Mix means take those tracks, pick your favorite ones, arrange them any way you want in a playlist to listen to your music the way you wanted to listen to it, not the way somebody put it together on an album at a record company. And burn means to take that favorite playlist and burn it on a CD so you can play it in your portable disc player or your car stereo, what have you. Rip Mix Burn. Now, just in case, I don't want anybody to get confused in this presentation. I'm going to use some some different words up here that I hope can't confuse anyone. Acquire, manage and listen. We're going to use those throughout the rest of the presentation.

Now, listen of course doesn't just mean burning a CD. You can listen to music on your computer as most of us do and of course now we have the iPod to listen to it on the go. So, we're going to start by focusing on listening and we're going to focus on the most exciting thing in listening and that's the iPod. It's been incredibly successful. We've sold 700,000 iPods since we launched it and it has become the number one MP3 player in the world.

Now, for those of us old enough, just like the Sony Walkman revolutionized portable music listening 20 years ago, in the digital age, the iPod is doing exactly the same thing. Now, can anyone ever top this? Well, we're going to try today because today we're introducing some new iPods. It's our third generation. No one's even caught up with our first generation yet and we're introducing our third. Three sizes, 10 gigabytes, 15 gigabytes and 30 gigabytes. The 30 gigabyte model holds 7500 songs in your pocket. A long way from the thousand songs in your pocket that we started with not long ago. And this is it. This is the new iPod. It is dramatically thinner at 0.62 inches and dramatically lighter at only 5.6 ounces. Now, how thin and light is that? That is lighter than the weight of two CDs in their jewel cases for 7500 songs versus 20 songs on the CDs. And it is thinner than those exact same two CDs. Yeah, it's wow.

So, thinner and lighter. Now, in addition, the no moving parts scroll wheel was so successful that we've made all the controls touch, no moving parts. And we have a much better screen now, much higher contrast ratio screen on the iPod. In addition to that, it has an incredibly nice backlight which lights up the buttons as well. So, the new iPod. Let's take a look at the top of it. We've got our headphone jack and the hold switch, but no firewire connector. We've put it on the bottom. There's the firewire connector and there's a cable that plugs right into it, but the iPod also drops into a dock. This has been one of the most requested features we've had. And so you can just drop your iPod in your dock and automatically connects to your computer so that you can sync, charge and go even faster and more conveniently. It's really, really nice. Now, just like cell phones and other devices, that connector that plugs into your iPod is the same connector that plugs into the dock, but look at what we've added on the dock. Line out. Another thing that has been heavily requested. People want to hook their iPods up to their stereos conveniently. There's a line out on the dock. You can even buy an accessory dock if you want, a second dock and put it right by your stereo so you can plug your iPod right in and charges and hooks up right to your stereo. We think this is going to be a strong feature. Now, iPods have always supported firewire. With these new iPods, we're adding USB2 for our Windows customers. Uh we got the hardware done, but the software is not quite done. There's a lot more testing to do on Windows. It's a little less predictable. And uh so we're going to have a software update in June, but the hardware is completely done. There's a cable that goes that connects into the iPod or the dock on one end and firewire on the other and that's included with every iPod since most customers we think are going to continue to use firewire. But for those that want to use USB, we have a cable with two plugs. Why is this? Because USB2 doesn't have enough power to power most things, including the iPod. So it can't charge from USB2. We have to ship a connector, a cable with a connector for USB2 to go into your computer and another connector for firewire to go into the charger. And for those customers that want it, that'll be $19 accessory cable because we don't want to burden all the firewire customers with an extra cable. The new iPods, like their predecessors, support Mac and Windows, but for the first time we're combining the models into one box so you can't get the wrong box. Mac and Windows in one box. So that's the hardware. What about the software? Well, of course we have auto sync. It's the one and only and because we have a ton of patents pending, we think it will stay the one and only. Uh and this is great. You just plug your iPod into your computer and your entire music library is automatically synchronized with your iPod. No one else does that. In addition, we're adding some new features. The first, heavily requested AAC decoding. AAC is a new code a new audio codec invented by Dolby. It's the best one in the industry and the iPod will now play AAC. Another big feature that was requested was on the go playlist. This is a playlist where you can actually build it right on your iPod. And personalizing the main menu. We're going to show you how to personalize the main menu so you can take the things you use the most and put them right up in the main menu. An alarm clock which will either give you a beep or will play your favorite playlist and two more new games, solitaire and parachute. Maybe the most important new feature of all. So, let me go ahead and show you some of this stuff. All right. Here's my iPod and uh the first thing I want to do is if we go into playlists, right at the bottom, you see the on the go playlist and if you go in there, what you'll see at first are some directions about how to set it up. So let's go back and uh let's go to uh let's go into browse and let's go into artists and I'll go into Bob Dylan who I love and uh we'll go into Blood on the Tracks and uh we'll pick Simple Twist of Fate and I just hold my finger down on the song and you see it flash? That just added it to the on the go playlist. And uh maybe I'll add uh if you see her say hello just by holding my finger down again. And maybe I'll go back and find another artist here. Uh maybe uh Counting Crows here and uh Hard Candy. I want the whole album so I'm just going to hold my finger down on the album and it flashes and I've added the whole album and if I go back up to the top and look in playlists and I look in my on the go playlist, you'll see Simple Twist of Fate, if you see her say hello and the entire album that I just added. Pretty simple.

Now, let me show you another really cool feature. I'm going to go into settings and we've added a new setting right under about called main menu. We put it right at the top because we think it's going to be very popular. And you go into main menu and it has all the key things with on or off toggles. So playlists I'm going to leave on, but browse, I don't I don't like to go to a second level to get artists. So I'm going to turn on artists and I'm going to turn on songs. And uh I don't want extras. All I really want is the clock and uh that's about it. So now I'm going to go to the top again and you'll see my menu is playlists, artists, songs, clock and settings. I can even go in there if I want and turn off playlists. And maybe I'll turn on uh maybe I'll turn on albums. And uh maybe I'll go down and say, you know, I I really like my contacts and uh I really like my games and I I know how to use the backlight now with the secret uh way to turn it on by holding down one of the keys. And so this is my new main menu. Pretty cool. And you can set it up and change it whenever you want. So, the new iPods. They are thinner and lighter. They have a really improved display in them with a great backlight. They have a dock. They have USB2 if you want it. They feature auto sync and the ability to have an on the go playlist and to change your main menu any way you want. Now, up until now, the most popular iPod has been the 10 gigabyte model. This has been the sweet spot at $399. We are lowering the cost of a 10 gigabyte iPod today to $299 for the new 10 gigabyte iPod. We have three models, the new 10, the new 15 and the new 30 gigabyte. 2500 songs in your pocket on the 10, 3700 on the 15 and 7500 on the 30. The 15 and the 30 have the dock, the case and the remote included. You can get these as accessories for the 10 if you want. And 299 for the 10, 399 for the 15 and 499 for the 20. When are these going to be available? They're going to be available this Friday across the US. Our whole channel is having some events this Friday and they're going to be a large supply of them this Friday. And they will be available one week later internationally, May 9th. So, the new iPod, clearly the best way now to listen to music. So,

Let's move on to manage. iTunes. We've had incredible success with this. Over 20 million copies of iTunes has been distributed and today we're on iTunes 3, but right now, we're introducing iTunes 4. iTunes 4 has got some cool new features in it. As you know, we support MP3 encoding and decoding, which is what a lot of people love to use. It's the most popular music format in the world, but we're also adding AAC encoding. And this is stuff that was pioneered by Dolby. It is actually the audio standard of the MPEG4 format. Now, why are we adding AAC? We're adding AAC alongside MP3 because AAC simply sounds a lot better than MP3 at any given bit rate. Matter of fact,

that we have built into Mac OS 10. And Rendezvous allows computers to find each other over any IP network, whether it's an Ethernet or an airport wireless network, find each other with zero configuration. So without setting anything up, typing in any names, these computers can find each other. And now iTunes is taking full advantage of it so that you can access playlists on other Macs and play the songs by streaming them over the network onto your Mac. Mac iTunes can now share playlists between Macs.

DVD archiving. You can now save your songs fully encoded, write them out to a DVD. Put about a thousand songs on a DVD, so if you want to back up your music library, you can. And if you have album artwork, you can drag it into iTunes now. So, four new features, iTunes 4 and I'd like to demo one of them, which is Rendezvous. So, I'm uh I'm at home using iTunes and uh let me go ahead and bring it up. And uh I'm uh you know, I could play a song if I want to. Now, my uh my son Phil comes home and uh Phil's got his new uh 12-inch PowerBook that I bought him. He's in college and uh within a few seconds now, watch what happens. Within a few seconds, our computers found each other over airport wireless networking and look at this. Here's Phil's playlist. When I click on it, it goes and gets all of his playlists and here are his playlists and I can pick uh favorites. I can go right into favorites and I just click on a song as if it was in my own library. Now, how's it getting that music? It's not copying it because that would be verboten. But we are streaming it. We are streaming it over the wireless networking from his iTunes to mine. Now, let's say Phil decides he's got to run back to his dorm room. He takes his iBook or PowerBook, closes it. Boom. Within a few seconds, the music and his playlists just go away. You know, but he he needs a loan so he comes back to talk to his dad, opens his, right? And uh within a few seconds, there is his uh Phil's PowerBook and uh here we go. And I can pick something else if I want. Now, my nephew uh Peter comes over and he's got his 12-inch PowerBook too and he goes ahead and opens it up and we'll see that in a few seconds Peter's going to pop up there all over airport wireless networking. There it is, right there, Peter's machine. Boom. It's getting his playlists. I can go to up and coming if I want to and uh pick anything I'd like. Isn't this cool?

All right. All right. Well, these guys got to go back to school, so they'll go ahead and shut their PowerBooks and we'll see this all go away. I don't retain any of the music on my computer, but I get all the enjoyment of listening to it when they're around. And so if you've got three Macs at your house and you are tired of uh having to give your CDs to other people and this and that, you can just share all your music with

---

## Part 2

**Steve Jobs**: between yourselves, as long as everybody's there on their computers, stream it across your wireless network or whatever network you have, using Rendezvous and iTunes 4. Zero configuration, no setup whatsoever.

**Steve Jobs**: So iTunes 4, AAC encoding and decoding, Rendezvous support, backup to DVD and album art, and we think that this is the best way to manage your music on the planet.

**Steve Jobs**: Which brings us to acquire.

**Steve Jobs**: Now, we acquire our music off CDs, right?

**Steve Jobs**: We go down and buy a CD and we rip it. But we all know that starting in 1999, there was this phenomenon called Napster, who was shut down in 2001, but it demonstrated some things for us. It demonstrated that the internet was made for music delivery.

**Steve Jobs**: And it's uh, it's offspring Kazaa is alive and well today, distributing lots of tracks. Now, there's a good side and a bad side of this. The good side is it offers users near instant gratification, at least as compared to going down to the record store, and again, shows that the internet was built for music delivery.

**Steve Jobs**: But the downside is it's stealing.

**Steve Jobs**: It is stealing.

**Steve Jobs**: So, from a user's point of view, let's look at the upsides and the downsides to this, from a user's point of view. First thing is, you've got a vast selection, better than any record store on the planet.

**Steve Jobs**: Unlimited CD burning.

**Steve Jobs**: Unlimited MP3 players. You can put the music on any number of them you want. You can put the music on an unlimited number of computers, and from a user's point of view, it's free. What's wrong with this? Right? It's fantastic. But there's a dark side to it.

**Steve Jobs**: Very unreliable downloads.

**Steve Jobs**: Very unreliable quality. A lot of these songs are encoded by seven-year-olds and they don't do a great job.

**Steve Jobs**: There are no previews. So you can spend a whole lot of time downloading a song and find out it's not exactly the one you wanted. No album cover art. And worst of all, it's stealing. It's best not to mess with karma.

**Steve Jobs**: So, most people don't focus on these things though. They focus on the good things. You can say, well, why has this proliferated? Well, because there's no legal alternative. There's no legal alternative that's worth beans. We say, well, what about Pressplay and Rhapsody? What about these things? Well, they're both subscription services.

**Steve Jobs**: You can't just go get a song and pay a little. You have to subscribe to them. And they don't even let you download all the songs, and they don't even let you put all the songs on your MP3 player. They don't let you burn a lot of CDs. Here's Pressplay. You if you do get some downloads, which you have to pay extra for, you can play them as long as your membership is active. So you you pay to download 500 songs and one day you stop paying your subscription fee and your entire music library goes away. Here's Rhapsody. Only subscribers to the all access subscription plan at 9.95 per month will get the ability to burn tracks, of course, for an additional fee per track.

**Steve Jobs**: These services treat you like a criminal.

**Steve Jobs**: And they are subscription based. And we think subscriptions are the wrong path. Now, one of the reasons we think this is because people have bought their music for as long as we can remember. We've bought our music on LPs, we've bought our music on cassettes, we've bought our music on CDs. And we think people want to buy their music on the internet by buying downloads just like they bought LPs, just like they bought cassettes, just like they bought CDs. They're used to buying their music and they're used to getting a broad set of rights with it. When you own your music, it never goes away. When you own your music, you have a broad set of personal use rights. You can listen to it however you want.

**Steve Jobs**: So, we decided since no one else was doing this, that we were going to do it. And we started about a year and a half ago to create a music store. Music downloads done right. Now, if we're going to compete with this, we're going to need a broad set of rights from the music companies. We need to go talk to the big five. The big five are the five biggest music companies in the world.

**Steve Jobs**: Here they are. Now, before we did this, I was reminded of a quote from Hunter S. Thompson about the music industry. The music business is a cruel and shallow money trench, a long plastic hallway where thieves and pimps run free and good men die like dogs. There's also a negative side.

So, we've gotten the uh URL applemusic.com. You'll be seeing it in a few places uh in the not too distant future and when you go there, it takes you right to the Apple website. Rock and roll will never die. It is, however, being reborn. And we also got some TV ads. These are hot off the presses, they're not done, but I want to share them with you to see what you think. And we wanted to really convey how much of a part of music, how much of a part of our lives music is. And uh so let's just go ahead and run some TV ads. See what you think of them.

So, there's one of those we may not run. Um, this is what we have for you today. New iPods, new iTunes 4 and the iTunes Music Store. And uh there's a lot of folks at Apple that have been working really hard on this stuff for the last 18 months and I'd like to give them a round of applause if that's okay.

So, the site is up. Have at it. Thank you very much for coming this morning. See you soon.
